“I trust you, Likud members, to choose your representatives correctly, according to your own judgment. I am not interfering in the national list, and I wish everyone success,” Netanyahu added.
Netanyahu pushed to change Likud’s long-standing primary system for selecting its Knesset slate
Likud has for years prided itself on conducting primaries in which its registered members are eligible to vote for the Knesset list. Netanyahu pushed to change the system in recent weeks ahead of the primaries, leading to an especially competitive race with even fewer slots available than usual.
Netanyahu was granted the authority to determine eight slots within the first 30 spots on the party list last month following a vote on the controversial decision by the Likud Central Committee.
There were reports that Netanyahu had threatened to leave Likud if the proposed changes were not advanced.
Those within the party who oppose changing the primaries have argued that it will cause those who would otherwise score highly in the primaries to fall further down the list.
The Likud primaries are further competitive because the party currently has around 40 ministers and MKs serving in the government and Knesset, but recent polls project the party winning only about 22 seats, leaving many at risk of losing their places on the party’s Knesset list.
The vote comes ahead of the general elections, which are set to take place on October 27. Parties are not required to hold primaries in Israel, and only a few do so.
Court rejects bid to ease Likud district primary restrictions ahead of vote
Further tensions surrounding the slots also come after the Tel Aviv District Court on Monday rejected Likud MK Afif Abed’s attempt to restore a narrowly approved change allowing current and former MKs, ministers and deputy ministers to run in the party’s district primaries, leaving the restrictions in place ahead of the vote.
Likud had announced last week that one of Netanyahu’s first reserved slots would go to entrepreneur and businessman Oren Dobronsky.
Additional reserved slots were later granted by Netanyahu to three ministers: Defense Minister Israel Katz, Foreign Minister Gideon Sa’ar, and Likud Central Committee Chairman Haim Katz, who also holds multiple ministerial portfolios.
The party said its internal court ruled that the defense minister should receive a reserved slot in order to “allow him to focus on security needs rather than engage in politics at this time.”
Likud also stated that Sa’ar would receive a reserved slot as part of the merger agreement between his party and Likud and that the Likud Central Committee chairperson would receive a slot due to his senior position in the party.
Sa’ar had announced in 2025 that his New Hope-United Right would be merging with Likud, and would be returning to the party. He previously resigned from Likud in 2020, heavily criticizing Netanyahu at the time.
The changes to the party’s primaries that have expanded Netanyahu’s control over the Knesset list have led to fierce internal tensions, with some party members in favor and others strongly against.
A fierce critic of changing the system has been MK Tally Gotliv, who is viewed as a candidate who would receive broad support from registered party members.
Gotliv has sharply criticized the Tuesday decision to reserve the slots for the three ministers, condemning the defense minister.
She called the decision to grant the defense minister a reserved slot “a disgraceful move that mocks Likud voters, who understand one thing more than all the veteran ministers: the need to fight the legal establishment that is persecuting the right-wing government and right-wing figures.”
Likud MK Amit Halevi calls upcoming primaries a ‘democratic celebration’
Likud MK Amit Halevi, who has expressed support for allowing the premier to reserve slots, told The Jerusalem Post that the primaries “will be a democratic celebration in the Likud.”
“I wish more parties conducted themselves democratically like the Likud. Some 140,000 members, active, engaged citizens who make their voices heard and have an influence, will go to the polls tomorrow,” he added.
“Together, God willing, we will put together a winning team that will be able to meet the national challenges ahead of us.”
“I am confident that Likud members will vote correctly for the sake of the country. The war exposed the many ills in the country’s systems, particularly the legal and security systems, which require fundamental reform. We will make those changes,” Halevi told the Post.
An internal Likud poll released on Sunday projected Gotliv, Knesset Speaker Amir Ohana, and Transportation Minister Miri Regev to rank among the top candidates in the primaries.
Likud primaries combine national, district, reserved slots to shape Knesset slate
The primaries determine the Likud’s Knesset slate, with the party chairman placed first. Registered members then vote for candidates on the national list, while members from geographic districts vote for candidates from their respective districts.
Candidates chosen on the national list are combined with district representatives and places that guarantee representation for groups including women, immigrants, young members, and minorities. The regulations also reserve certain positions for candidates chosen by the party chairman.
In the 2022 primaries, for example, the first group of positions after the party chairman was largely filled by nationally elected candidates, while district positions and guaranteed-representation slots were inserted farther down the slate. Netanyahu was also given several reserved positions.
The precise locations of those different categories are determined before each election through the party’s temporary election regulations. That is why the current fight has centered not only on whether primaries will take place, but on how much of the resulting slate the members will actually control.
Sarah Ben-Nun contributed to this report.

Here's what is changing about how food delivery workers are paid
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:55:16 UTC
03:55:16 KST

Food delivery workers to receive better pay under new minimum standards
In short:
New interim minimum standards for food and grocery delivery workers come into effect today, improving conditions on pay and insurance.
It will see workers for platforms such as Uber Eats and DoorDash receive at least $31.30 an hour for engaged time, above the national minimum wage of $26.44.
It comes after the Albanese government introduced gig economy reforms two years ago that gave new powers to the Fair Work Commission.
Gig worker Alexi Edwards spends roughly 40 hours on the road delivering orders every week. At times, she says her pay was as low as $15 an hour.
It has left the 30-year-old anxious and uncertain as the cost of rent and bills rise.
"In those moments you ask yourself why you're doing this, it's not the best feeling," Ms Edwards told the ABC.
But she hopes Australia's first minimum standards for gig economy workers, which come into effect today, will provide some level of stability for her and others.
The changes are expected to affect about 250,000 workers, and will see food and grocery delivery drivers receive higher pay and new insurance protection.
The federal government's gig worker reforms were introduced two years ago, which empowered the Fair Work Commission to set minimum standards for "employee-like" contractors.
Until now, most gig workers operated as independent contractors, which put them outside of many workplace protections available to employees.
The Transport Workers Union's (TWU) national secretary Michael Kaine described the changes as a decade in the making.
"It's history in the making really, not just in Australia, but right around the world,"
"[When] the gig economy came into Australia in about 2012 and it engaged workers as independent contractors, it pushed them outside of the protections that have been built up for years."
What are the new minimum standards?
The changes under the Fair Work Commission order for food delivery drivers will see a new "interim" minimum standard order, which will create an earnings floor.
Workers for platforms such as Uber Eats and DoorDash will receive at least $31.30 an hour for engaged time, above the national minimum wage of $26.44.
The minimum hourly rate for engaged time, which was the period between accepting and completing a delivery, differs depending on the choice of vehicle:
- E-bikes $31.30 an hour
- Motorcycles $31.80 an hour
- Cars $32 an hour
To ensure food delivery drivers are paid the earnings floor for their engaged time working, platforms will need to calculate a worker's total earnings over a 21-day period.
It means platforms will need to increase a workers' pay if they are paid on average less than the earnings floor.
Workers will not be paid for the time waiting for a new delivery job but will be paid for time waiting at restaurants for orders they have already accepted.
Under the new standards, there have also been changes to insurance arrangements between platform and workers.
Workers are still required to cover the costs of insurance for their vehicles but now platforms will need to offer a reasonable minimum level of personal accident cover.
Platforms must also now consult and notify workers about significant changes such as exiting the market.
Other changes brought by the new standards include:
- a new feedback forum for workers to raise concerns
- a new procedure for resolving disputes
- a right to unpaid time away
How we got to the new standards
Following a ruling by the Fair Work Ombudsman in 2019, gig economy workers have been classified as independent contractors rather than employees.
Loading...
It has meant gig workers did not have access to employee entitlements such as minimum wage, annual leave, sick leave or other benefits.
But in 2024, the Albanese government passed the 'Closing Loopholes' reforms which legislated protections for some gig economy workers such as food delivery drivers.
It gave the Fair Work Commission new powers to regulate the gig economy with minimum standards that are legally enforceable.
University of Sydney's Dr Alex Veen, who specialises in employment relations, said in the two years since the legislation passed, the union and platforms such as Uber Eats and DoorDash have been in negotiations.
Before the government passed the new laws both delivery platforms said it could lead to price increases of at least 85 per cent.
Associate Professor Veen said despite initial concerns, the new minimum standards were agreed after a consensus was reached between all parties.
"It's very pleasing to see that it's gone through a process of cooperation and negotiation rather than 'we've had an outcome that was enforced by the commission',"
"It's created mechanisms and opportunities for workers to better engage with the platforms.
"It's not necessary that it's been a very costly type of order that's been developed, but one that has given a lot more certainty to workers."
Uber Eats' managing director Ed Kitchen said the reform maintained the flexibility of gig work while also improving conditions for workers.
"These standards provide a guaranteed safety net while protecting the flexibility delivery people tell us they value most," Uber Eats Australia and New Zealand managing director Mr Kitchen said.
A DoorDash spokesperson said the new minimum standards were an example of what happens when industry and unions find common ground.
"This is modern regulation that will protect workers without regulating away the flexibility that brought them to the work in the first place," a spokesperson said.
Professor Veen added the new minimum standards were only an interim order given by the Fair Work Commission, and could also change.
"So they are a starting point that will allow us to further evaluate whether or not this is actually both sustainable from a worker and an organisational perspective.
"It's effectively a living document."
What it means for food delivery drivers
Ms Edwards has already calculated how many engaged hours she works, at roughly 30 hours a week.
The new minimum standards mean she can begin to slow down, rather than continue to rush from job to job to make enough for decent pay.
Ms Edwards said riding her e-bike in Brisbane when she's having to make multiple orders can feel unsafe at times.
According to the Transport Worker's Union at least 25 gig workers have died since 2017.
"The roads are not built for bikes and it's pretty clear to tell. It can get quite scary sometimes,"
"[But now] I'd be able to live life not just on the edge. I'd be able to like plan, and it just makes it all a lot more sustainable in the long run."
Ms Edwards said the minimum standards should not just include food delivery workers.
"It should extend to the entire gig economy with this just being the first step," she said.

Mining, business leaders warn immigration changes could discourage skilled migrant workers
In short:
Business and mining groups are resisting a push to curb migration, warning skilled workers are critical to the health of the economy.
Australian Industry Group boss Innes Willox says Australia is in a "war for talent" and needed to be "responsible but as welcoming as possible".
What's next?
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is expected to unveil cuts to the government's immigration program after initially cancelling a speech on the topic earlier this month.
Powerful business and mining groups are resisting a push across the political spectrum to slash migration, warning Australia needs a steady flow of workers to deliver on a pipeline of projects and keep the economy moving.
The government is poised to cut migration and is considering forcing skilled migrants' families to be processed offshore, while the shadow housing minister has backed "modest" cuts focused on backpackers and international students.
It was later revealed his shadow cabinet colleagues had not been consulted on the proposal.
One Nation's leader Pauline Hanson said earlier this month she does "not care" what effect sweeping migration cuts would have on businesses, sticking with the party's line to significantly cut the intake to give Australia a "breather".
Australian Industry Group boss Innes Willox said he was "enormously concerned" about suggestions the government or other parties were considering tinkering with migration in a way which would discourage workers from coming to Australia.
"We are in a global war for talent, and we need to be as responsible but as welcoming as possible,"
He said a number of big projects including the Olympics build in Queensland would not get done without skilled migrant labour, warning the immigration system must have "integrity and value".
"That's for the migrant, the employer, their family, and the economy as a whole," he said.
Minerals Council boss Tania Constable said her members needed about 40,000 new migrant workers over the next three years to resource existing and approved projects.
She said while she supported the goal of securing services and housing to meet the needs of Australians, migrant workers were critical to keeping the economy going.
"Across the board, we have a shortage," she said.
"We need those workers, and we need them pretty quickly."
Migrant workers indispensable to mining sector
Chamber of Minerals and Energy WA chief executive Aaron Morey said the mining sector was already struggling to source workers and could not afford to "go backwards".
"Migrant workers are more important to the WA economy than they are to any other economy in the country," he said.
"The important thing for us is that we don't go backwards. It would make a difficult situation even harder to manage."
Ms Constable said the number of migrant workers in the minerals sector had more than doubled since 2021, but the industry was still experiencing shortages.
The government's current permanent migration intake is 185,000 places, about 70 per cent of which are skilled workers, with the majority of the remainder their families.
The Coalition has not released its proposed migration numbers aside from a promise to tie it to housing completions.
In an interview last week, One Nation leader Pauline Hanson said she wants to reduce the 185,000 permanent migration number to 130,000.
The party has not nominated which visa streams would be subject to its 130,000 target, except for 75,000 people they said are in Australia illegally.
Mining magnate Gina Rinehart, who owns Hancock Industries in WA, has thrown her support behind One Nation.
Ms Constable said while she could not comment on the specific numbers put forward by the party, she would continue to advocate for all parties to "get the balance right".
"We will ensure that we present of all the policy options that we think are right for our industry … and we will do that without prejudice and without favour," she said.
Mr Morey said Mrs Rinehart's support of One Nation did not impact the industry's ability to criticise certain policies.
"Absolutely not," he said.
"Irrespective of which party and political persuasion, what is important to maintain our sector is to ideally increase and at least maintain the number of skilled migration."
Government slows intake of working holidays visas
Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke yesterday confirmed the government had quietly slowed the intake of working holiday visa applications but did not explain why.
"They are still being processed, but they are being processed more slowly than they were previously," he said.
Mr Willox said temporary workers, including those on working holiday visas, were a "central" part of the Australian workforce particularly in regional communities and agriculture.
"They play really important gap filler role in the economy, and it shouldn't be underestimated," he said.
"Business don't need permanent labour; they need temporary labour to fill a need and that is where temporary workers play a really important role."
Mr Burke said the primary visas used in the agricultural industry were the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) scheme visa, which is a scheme for workers from the Pacific and Timor-Leste.
"One of the things that happened when we started to improve the worker protections on PALM was, not overwhelmingly, but some of the worst operators said if we've got to have standards to PALM workers, we will just switch to backpackers.
"And that is not the way this system is meant to work."

US men and Canada women win flag football world titles as spots earned for the Los Angeles Olympics
DÜSSELDORF, Germany (AP) — The United States successfully defended the men’s title at the flag football world championships on Sunday but lost the women’s title to Canada, while Mexico’s women and Canada’s men earned qualification spots for the 2028 Olympic Games in Los Angeles.
The U.S. men beat Italy 46-26 to secure a sixth straight title and the women missed out on a fourth straight title after losing 27-20 to Canada.
“Gold is the only standard,” said men’s quarterback Nico Casares, who threw two touchdown passes. “That’s our motto. That’s what we play by, that’s what we live by.”
The U.S. women started strongly but it was tied 14-14 at the break after Caroline Moquin-Joubert caught quarterback Sara Parker’s pass at the end of the first half. Parker set up Frederique Morneau at the start of the second half as Canada took control.
The U.S. had a fourth down, yards from the line, with three seconds left, but could not make the final play count. It was Canada’s third title and first since beating the U.S. in the 2014 final.
“I feel so happy, I can’t believe it,” Parker said after hugging her mother. ”Literally the best day ever.”
The International Federation of American Football ran the championship tournament, which doubled up as a qualifier, in the German city of Düsseldorf.
The top two men’s and top two women’s teams earned a spot at the 2028 Games, along with the U.S. men’s and women’s teams because they already qualified as hosts.
Sunday’s two other finalists — the Italian men and Canadian women — earned an Olympic spot by reaching the final against the U.S. teams, meaning that the bronze-medal games decided who joined them.
Mexico women cried with joy after a 20-19 win over Great Britain — which rallied from 20-6 down — for the women’s bronze and an Olympic spot.
But Mexico’s men lost 34-26 in overtime to Canada, which claimed an Olympic spot.
Rules of the game
Flag football was among five sports given Olympic status for the 2028 Games back in 2023, with the game played five-on-five in two 20-minute halves, no tackling and an emphasis on speed and elusiveness.
The NFL has said it plans to launch women’s and men’s professional flag football ahead of the Olympics. ___

The 30-year policy collision behind Australia's housing crunch
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:45:00 UTC
03:45:00 KST

analysis
A big part of the problem with housing in Australia, and the rest of the economy, is a slow-moving collision that began under the Howard government between the regulation of housing and the effective deregulation of migration in the early 2000s.
Migration was deregulated to address the aging of Australia's population as well as skills shortages while also being left to the market — largely demand-driven and with no targets on the overall level, only permanent migration. At the same time, construction was much more heavily regulated.
As a result, net migration increased while housing construction did the opposite. Over 30 years, these two sets of policies compounded and created the housing affordability crisis we have today.
These policies were introduced by different Labor and Coalition governments, but all presumably went through various PM's offices and cabinets for approval. The result is a classic set of unintended consequences and, with housing, a crisis.
From 1995, the Keating and Howard governments streamlined temporary migration by progressively making it demand-driven rather than based on quotas or policy targets.
Likewise, with the steady growth in the size and complexity of Australian building codes, and then the National Construction Code.
The first step was visas
Let's start with migration reforms, with July 1, 2001 and 2022 as key dates.
The first is important because of student visa reforms, and the second because the Coalition government had stomped on the immigration accelerator in its final years, leading to a blow-out in 2022-24.
Many argue the new Labor government has taken too long to start putting on the brakes.
But the first step came with the 457 visa, introduced in August 1996 as the Temporary Business (Long Stay) visa. In March 2018, the 457 visa was abolished and replaced by the Temporary Skill Shortage visa (482).
The Howard Coalition government created 457 visas following the recommendations of the 1995 Roach Report. The inquiry was commissioned by the Keating Labor government and headed by Neville Roach, a former executive with IBM and Fujitsu, to streamline business migration.
The 457 program ended up at the laissez-faire end of temporary labour migration schemes globally, with a total absence of quotas, caps, or labour market testing. In 2013, they were revamped slightly along with the name change to 482 visas, which suggested the reforms were greater than they were.
But the system was fatally undermined by setting the minimum salary at $53,000 and then leaving it for a decade with no indexation.
The result was that when the labour market tightened in 2022 after the pandemic, the number of 482 visas exploded as businesses went for cheap labour.
However, construction trades were explicitly excluded. Some say it was at the behest of the CFMEU, which was negotiating an EBA at the time (although that has never been confirmed).
On top of loose 457 visas that almost entirely excluded tradies, a flood of student visas followed.
The role of universities
On July 1, 2001, these were made "country neutral" instead of being categorised by whether the student came from a "gazetted" or "non-gazetted" country. The latter group included India, China and other Asian countries. The former included Europe, the UK and the US.
The new system categorised the applications under the institution, not the country, which was a worthwhile change, but it resulted in many of these visas being issued. That's because permanent residency was added.
It was decreed that international students who completed a degree in Australia in an occupation on the Migration Occupations in Demand List (MODL) — such as IT, accounting, or specific trades — were permitted to apply for permanent residency onshore under the Skilled-Independent category without leaving the country. The standard post-graduate work experience requirement was waived entirely.
Applicants also received five bonus points on the points test for their Australian qualification and were required to apply within six months of course completion.
The stated policy goal, from the Department of Immigration, was to "further assist the entry of successful overseas students to the Australian labour market", effectively using universities as a kind of pre-selection mechanism, since graduates already had local qualifications, some English proficiency, and local work experience.
This transformed international education into Australia's second biggest export industry, but it also meant that a large part of Australia's migration policy was outsourced to universities desperate for cash.
Universities became migration gatekeepers. A guaranteed pathway to permanent residency directly incentivised course selection by prospective students. Universities went for it, recruiting students from around the world using commission agents paid as much as 30 per cent of the first year's tuition fee.
Net overseas migration attributable to the student visa stream rose from 45,250 in 2004-05 to 108,740 in 2007-08, a gain of 63,490 people, accounting for 47 per cent of all NOM growth over that period.
But this did not result in more construction trades because the students from Asian countries were not doing apprenticeships; they were doing degrees.
And 457 visas did not result in more tradies either because Australia's trades qualification authorities did not fully recognise their qualifications.
Enter the backpacker
And then there are the backpackers.
The liberalisation of the working holiday maker visa (subclass 417) came on November 1, 2005, when the government introduced the "second-year visa" initiative, letting first-time 417 holders extend their stay by a further 12 months if they spent 88 days (three months) in regional areas doing specified work in agriculture, mining, fishing, or construction.
This was explicitly designed as a labour market intervention to fill gaps in the horticulture labour force (fruit and veggie pickers), of which there was a genuine shortage.
And then on July 1, 2019, the Morrison government introduced a further extension: a working holiday maker who had already got a second-year visa by doing 88 days of regional work could qualify for a third year by completing an additional six months (179 days) of specified regional work during that second year.
The construction-climate link
While all this was going on in the early 2000s, eventually leading to an explosion in immigration, the Howard government started using building regulations as the primary response to climate change.
It was before the Coalition became rather more sceptical about climate change. This approach resulted from a 1998 document entitled National Greenhouse Strategy, endorsed by all Australian governments.
The policy dated back to the Kyoto Protocol in 1997, which the Howard government refused to sign but instead produced a report arguing that a range of new housing regulations were needed to address global warming through energy efficiency in the built environment.
On July 19, 2000, the Howard government announced an agreement with the states and territories to develop national energy efficiency provisions for domestic and commercial buildings.
Six months later, the Australian Greenhouse Office and the Australian Building and Construction Board developed a series of energy efficiency measures to include in the Building Code of Australia, the forerunner to the National Construction Code.
The stated intention was to reduce greenhouse gas emissions by making houses cooler in summer and warmer in winter, reducing reliance on artificial heating and cooling.
The housing industry broadly supported the changes and accepted a mandatory approach because it provided a level playing field. They also felt that regulations should be consolidated into what was then the Building Code of Australia wherever possible so there was one national code instead of a patchwork of state energy regulations.
The first change was amendment 13 to the BCA, which came into force on July 1, 2003, introducing energy efficiency provisions for Class 1 (houses). It was explicitly the first stage of a gradual national rollout, not a one-off.
In 2005, it was extended to all residential buildings, and then in 2006, it was expanded to all remaining building classifications. Housing stringency was lifted to a five-star target.
In 2010, this was strengthened again to six stars for both commercial and residential buildings under the National Strategy on Energy Efficiency and then later to seven stars.
In 2013, the BCA was rebranded as the National Construction Code and the Plumbing Code was incorporated into it as Volume Three.
Further big changes to the NCC then happened in 2022 under the new Labor government, with mandatory accessibility provisions included for the first time to go with NDIS.
New condensation management provisions were also added as part of Australia's 2015 Paris Agreement emissions commitments and the National Energy Productivity Plan.
The NCC then picked up new EV rules, with a requirement that buildings accommodate electric vehicle charging, and tightened wet-weather details such as a minimum 15mm freeboard height for valley gutters.
In 2025, there was another refinement but not a rewrite, including more stringent condensation provisions and electric vehicle pre-provisioning requirements for all new homes, plus another suite of commercial energy efficiency stringency increases.
Then this year, with the National Housing Accord supply targets falling short and the industry getting increasingly agitated about the size and complexity of the NCC, the Albanese government asked the Productivity Commission to review housing regulations, although the NCC was explicitly excluded.
Separately, in another report, the PC revealed the idea of subjecting changes to the NCC to cost-benefit analysis had been abandoned, and that it had become a tool for social and environmental policy, rather than setting basic standards for safety, amenity, waterproofing and structural integrity.
Loading
Compounding impact
The growth in the amount and complexity of building regulations was not a single event but a compounding series of well-meant measures by both sides of politics that nobody connected to the cost of building a house.
Adding to this was the simultaneous growth of land use zoning and planning regulations at the state level, with no connection to national housing supply needs or construction feasibility.
On top of that was progressive deregulation and a complete lack of control over temporary migration, which has resulted in 2,807,322 temporary migrants currently living in Australia — a million more than five years ago — while construction productivity and the size of the construction workforce have sunk to record lows.
The crisis was inevitable.
Alan Kohler is a finance presenter and columnist on ABC News. He hosts the podcast That’s Business with Alan Kohler in the ABC Business Daily feed on Friday. He also writes for Intelligent Investor.
Editor's note, August 17: This story was updated to reflect the Productivity Commission was asked by the Albanese government to review housing regulations but the NCC was explicitly excluded. It was a separate PC research paper that covered the NCC.

Brazil’s Lula launches historic fourth term bid – but son of jailed Bolsonaro stands in his way
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:44:41 UTC
03:44:41 KST

Brazil’s leftwing president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has launched his campaign for a historic fourth term and vowed that as long as he lived he would not allow the “shameless” right to return to power.
Addressing a sea of supporters in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where his political career began nearly half a century ago, the 80-year-old politician reminded voters of the chaos and violence that unfolded during the 2018-22 presidency of his far-right predecessor, Jair Bolsonaro, whose son Flávio Bolsonaro will face Lula in October’s presidential election.
Lula recalled how hundreds of thousands of citizens died during a Covid outbreak Jair Bolsonaro was accused of bungling with his anti-science policies. Gun ownership soared as laws were relaxed, allowing criminal groups to expand their arsenals. “They handed out … more than a million weapons,” Lula said, promising to dedicate a fourth term to improving education and healthcare as well as developing Brazil’s rare-earth deposits, the world’s second largest after China’s.
Lula also said he would improve security by targeting the rich organised crime bosses who lived in luxury apartments. “It’s easy to kill a crook in a favela. But the guy running the show lives in a penthouse … and we need to stop this,” Lula said. He also told his far-right rivals to “show some shame”.
Lula was speaking at the Vila Euclides football stadium, where his astonishing rise to the presidency began in 1979 when, as 33-year-old union leader, he spearheaded two historic strikes that helped end the military dictatorship. Those strikes made Lula a household name and in 2002, after three failed attempts, he won a landslide victory to become his country’s first working-class president.
During Lula’s first two-terms, from 2002 until 2010, he was credited with fighting hunger, dramatically expanding social welfare programmes and access to higher education, and improving Brazil’s global standing, although his administration was blighted by corruption scandals. His successor, Dilma Rousseff, became Brazil’s first female president but led the country into a severe economic recession before being controversially impeached in 2016.
In 2018, Lula was jailed for alleged corruption and he spent 580 days in prison before the supreme court quashed his conviction. Lula’s imprisonment allowed Bolsonaro to win that year’s election, ushering in four years of environmental destruction and international isolation.
In 2022 Lula won his third term, defeating Bolsonaro by a razor-thin margin and vowing to rescue the country from “one of the worst periods in Brazilian history”. “This nightmare is over,” Lula declared at his January 2023 inauguration. A week later, far-right radicals rampaged through the capital, Brasília, in a botched attempt to bring Bolsonaro back.
Bolsonaro was jailed in 2025 for 27 years for plotting that failed post-election power grab. Flávio Bolsonaro, a 45-year-old senator, launched his campaign on Sunday with an event on Rio’s Copacabana beach, previously the scene of huge rallies in support of his father. “I am going to be Brazil’s next president because I’m going to fight this system,” Bolsonaro, who wore a bullet-proof vest under a yellow Brazil shirt, told a crowd far smaller than those his father used to attract.
Polls suggest Lula holds a slender advantage over Bolsonaro, with 43% of intended votes to his rival’s 40% in a run-off which will take place on 25 October if, as expected, no candidate secures 50% of the vote in the 4 October first round.
André Pagliarini, the author of a book about Lula called A People’s President and the Fight for Brazil’s Future, said the showdown would be “the single most important electoral contest this year in the world”.
Pagliarini said he believed a Bolsonaro victory would be a significant boost for the pro-Trump “reactionary block” that has won elections across Latin America, from Argentina and Chile to Colombia, where the far-right lawyer Abelardo de la Espriella recently took office.
Donald Trump’s administration has repeatedly asserted its leadership over the region, launching deadly military operations against alleged “narco-terrorists” in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific, threatening to “take back” the Panama canal and, in January, abducting Venezuela’s dictator, Nicolás Maduro. Last week, the US state department published an incendiary video declaring that “American dominance in the western hemisphere will never be questioned again”.
In recent months Trump has turned up the heat on Brazil, designating its two biggest organised crime groups, the Red Command and the PCC, as terrorist organisations. That has kindled fears of a US military intervention on Brazilian soil or interference in Brazil’s presidential election.
During a visit to a jungle training camp in Panama on Friday, Trump’s defence secretary, Pete Hegseth, said Washington planned to use the military to “ruthlessly” pursue Latin American drug traffickers, “just like [they did with] Isis and al-Qaida” during the “war on terror”.
The idea, Hegseth said, was to “do bad things to bad people – because for too long, bad people did bad things to good people inside the United States of America and across Central and South America”.
There was anger at the US outside Lula’s campaign launch on Sunday, where some activists handed out stickers that read: “Fuck Trump.”
Seixas Alves, a 33-year-old Lula supporter, said he worried the decision to classify Brazilian drug factions as terrorist groups could be used as a pretext for a US attack. “Just like they [did with] Saddam Hussein,” Alves added, referring to the Iraqi dictator’s supposed development of weapons of mass destruction.
In Rio, Flávio Bolsonaro praised Trump’s decision to target the Brazilian crime groups and said he was the only politician capable of “sitting down with the US”.
In Vila Euclides, Simone Tebet, a centrist Lula ally, urged voters to do everything they could to stop Brazil falling back into the hands of far-right politicians who wanted “to kill Brazilian democracy” and create “a country of hate”.

More than 100,000 without power in Hawaii as Lala downgraded to tropical storm
HILO, Hawaii - Almost 130,000 utility customers in Hawaii had no power on the morning of Aug 16 after Hurricane Lala brushed the Big Island before being downgraded to a tropical storm.
Data from poweroutageus.com as of 4.35am HST (10.35pm in Singapore) indicated that most of the affected areas were on the Big Island, Honolulu County and Maui County.
Hawaiian Electric warned customers on the evening of Aug 15 that the repair efforts were hampered by the hurricane-force winds and rain, citing flooded roadways and downed trees.
Video released by the Hawaii Department of Transportation showed flood waters overtaking roads.
Authorities reported one dead in a car-related incident.
Two homes were swept away, according to the National Weather Service.
Big Island resident Cynthia Totty-Hefley said on Aug 15 she had “a little anxiety” about rising water.
“What I’m most worried about is... the ocean coming into my house,” she told local station KITV.
An advisory from the National Hurricane Centre at 2am HST predicted another 10cm to 20cm of rain on the Big Island and windward Maui, which would mean as much as 76cm to 89cm overall since Lala started lashing Hawaii late on Aug 14.
Though the storm barely skirted landfall, Governor Josh Green cautioned islanders to shelter in place as forecasters warned of substantial damage.
Although US weather officials downgraded Lala to a tropical storm, its maximum sustained winds of 112kmh were just below hurricane status.
The hurricane centre continued to warn of “life-threatening” conditions. Lala’s maximum sustained winds on Aug 16 reached 120kmh, making it a Category 1 hurricane.
The Hawaii Department of Transportation said on Aug 15 it closed Hilo International Airport and Ellison Onizuka Kona International Airport, with both expected to reopen on Aug 16. State officials advised travellers to check with their airlines for updates. REUTERS

As solar panel waste grows, extra installation fee proposed to fund recycling
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:40:22 UTC
03:40:22 KST

Recycling fee put forward as solution to Australia's growing solar panel waste
In short:
The Australian Academy of Technological Sciences & Engineering has called for a national reuse and recycling scheme for solar panels that would add about $10 to the cost of each panel at installation.
The proposal was made during a federal inquiry into solar panel waste but some experts say recycling could cost more due to transport and logistics.
What's next?
A national solar panel recycling pilot program due to begin mid this year is yet to start.
One of Australia's leading science organisations says an additional installation fee of about $10 for each panel could help solve Australia's rooftop solar waste problem.
However, experts fear the cost of recycling the waste products could exceed the funds generated by the fee, due to transport and logistics costs.
At present, one in three homes in Australia has rooftop solar, with about 300,000 systems being installed annually.
But only 17 per cent of solar panels are recycled, according to the Productivity Commission.
During a parliamentary inquiry into solar panel reuse and recycling, the Australian Academy of Technological Sciences & Engineering (ATSE) called for a national recycling scheme for used solar panels, funded by a fee of between $10 and $20 for each panel at installation.
Acting CEO Peter Derbyshire said ATSE recommended establishing a solar panel product stewardship scheme that shifted cost and responsibility to manufacturers, importers and customers.
"Currently there is no framework around product stewardship for solar panels,"
In 2017 the federal government put on a list of national priorities "establishing a product stewardship scheme for solar panels", a scheme that would manage the life cycle of products.
In January, Energy Minister Chris Bowen announced a pilot program for national solar panel recycling, which was suppose to begin in mid-2026.
But a spokesperson from the Department of Climate Change, Energy, the Environment and Water (DCCEEW) said procurement of the program had not been completed.
"The government remains committed to the pilot," a DCCEEW spokesperson said in a statement.
How big of a problem is solar panel waste?
Australia generates about 60,000 tonnes of solar panel waste every year, and the federal government projects that figure could rise to 90,000 by 2030.
By comparison, in 2023-24, Australia generated 27 million tonnes of building and demolition waste, 15 million tonnes of organic waste and 10 million tonnes of coal ash, according to the National Waste and Resource Recovery Report 2024.
Australian National University's professor Andrew Blakers, who specialises in solar systems, said solar panel waste was a small issue.
"At the moment, solar panel waste is about one fifth of 1 per cent of the solid waste stream in Australia,"
"It is about 5 kilograms per person per year, which is a very, very small amount of waste compared with even household waste, let alone commercial industrial waste."
He added that outside of the metal frame and cables, about 90 per cent of a solar panel was glass.
"Glass is an incredibly cheap and safe waste material," he said.
"A solar panel is actually almost equivalent to a windscreen, which is also a laminated glass structure. Both can simply be crushed and put in landfill without any significant problems."
Even in the worst-case scenario, researchers from the US National Renewable Energy Laboratory projected about 160,000 million tonnes of solar panel waste would be generated between 2016 and 2050 worldwide.
In comparison, municipal and coal ash waste was tipped to hit a combined total of 100 billion tonnes over the same period.
How do recycling schemes work overseas?
University of Sydney's Penelope Crossley, who specialises in legal issues associated with the energy transition, examined recycling schemes in more than 100 jurisdictions worldwide.
Professor Crossley said in Europe the cost of recycling a solar panel was "broadly comparable" with the $10 to 20 per-panel estimate cited by the ATSE.
European estimates put the cost at about €300 to €500 ($490 to $815) per tonne, but that was not the final cost, she said.
Collection, transport and processing affected the cost.
"Transport alone [is] estimated to account for around 10 to 15 per cent of recycling costs,"
"In regional and remote areas of Australia, this could add significant cost. It can be very easy to forget that a regulatory solution not only has to work in Sydney, but also in Wilcannia."
The European Union's waste electrical and electronic equipment directive placed the responsibility of solar panels on producers, she said.
It meant the regulation required them to finance the collection and treatment of solar panels at the end of their life.
"The cost is built into the regulatory framework rather than simply falling on the household or business disposing of the panel," Professor Crossley said.
She said a challenge she had witnessed in other jurisdictions was laws and regulations having unintended consequences for solar panel recycling.
"We don't automatically assume that a solar panel being taken off a roof is going to be waste.
"We need to think about whether that solar panel could be reused as an interim step in the process."
Could it lead to a more circular economy?
Some experts say a stewardship scheme could help create a more circular economy.
Those schemes can take a few forms: it can be a co-regulatory partnership between industry and government, led by industry through voluntary arrangement, or mandatory under the law.
University of Melbourne's circular economy chair Damien Giurco said several products had stewardship schemes including TVs, computers, oil, plastics and packaging and others.
Loading...
Professor Giurco said it was sensible to have a solar panel scheme from the moment of installation.
"Otherwise, if you look to when people are getting rid of the solar panels, asking people to pay then is trickier," he said.
"So I think this idea of setting it up so that there's a little bit of money, a little deposit that can see the rest of the system runs well.
"I mean, it's got some parallels in a bigger sense to the way you get 10 cents on your Coke can."
The economic benefits of recycling solar panels could provide real economic benefits, according to researchers at the University of Adelaide.
The study found the recycling industry could generate up to $US670.8 billion ($950.6 billion) globally by 2060.
"We need to think of solar panels as part of a circular economy rather than a disposable product," professor Jian Zuo, co-author of the study, said.
Unlike in Europe, Professor Crossley said, Australia should have a user-pay system because renewable energy subsidies favoured high to middle-income earners.
She said solar panel recycling was necessary, but the challenge included ensuring solutions were economically efficient and made environmental sense.
The worst-case scenario at present was sending solar panels to landfill, knowing they contained elements worth stockpiling in future such as polysilicon, silver and others, Professor Crossley said.
"You don't want solar panels being stockpiled at warehouses either.
"You're not going to get piles of solar panel fires, but they're just big and bulky and we need to come up with a better solution."

Iranian researcher recounts ordeal of arbitrary US detention
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:40:17 UTC
03:40:17 KST

Despite holding valid legal status and residing in the US for 13 years, Azizi was subjected to a pre-dawn raid on April 13 outside his Maryland home.
Speaking to Press TV on Sunday following his voluntary return to Iran, Azizi detailed a harrowing ordeal marked by baseless allegations, inhumane detention conditions, and a clear effort to silence his vocal criticism of US and Israeli foreign policy.
Azizi recounted the morning of his arrest, which occurred shortly after he dropped his children off at school. Rather than standard ICE officers, the operation was led by heavily armed FBI agents.
"There were more than ten cars assigned by the FBI. When I stepped out of my car, they had all their rifles pointed at me," Azizi said. He was subsequently handed over to ICE and taken to a detention center in Baltimore.
During his three-month detention, interrogators repeatedly pressed him on a baseless claim that he was a member of the Student Basij Organization, a branch within the IRGC-affiliated Basij Organisation for university campuses, during his first master’s degree.
Authorities attempted to weaponize the US government’s 2019 designation of the IRGC as a terrorist organization, retroactively demanding he disclose this alleged affiliation from years prior.
"It is completely baseless," Azizi stated. "We had two or three court hearings, and they never showed any proof. They claimed to have 'multiple resources,' which were clearly anti-Islamic Republic propaganda outlets, but they never provided a shred of evidence."
Beyond the fabricated charges, Azizi described a grueling and deliberately punishing transfer process designed to break detainees.
Over a span of six days, he was forcibly moved from Maryland to Louisiana, then to Arizona, and finally to California.
"This is not just about me; it is the ICE process and the business model behind it, involving private contractors," Azizi explained. "When they transfer you, you are not just handcuffed; you are shackled by your legs. For 12 to 13 hours, you are in the belly of an airplane. It is horrible."
He detailed being held in a temporary, freezing detention center in Arizona with 30 other people in a small room for two nights without pillows or adequate facilities, leading to severe health deterioration among the detainees.
Azizi’s detention sparked outrage within the American academic community.
His legal team presented the immigration judge with a staggering 250 pages of support letters from professors at the University of Michigan, Harvard University, Virginia Tech, and other institutions, vouching for his character and academic integrity.
However, Azizi noted that the immigration court system is heavily influenced by the Department of Justice.
Just hours before his bond hearing, the FBI submitted a flimsy, two-page memo alleging national security risks and claiming he was a "prominent member" of the Basij.
The judge, bound by administrative directives, denied his release.
Azizi believes his media presence made him a target. As a regular commentator on outlets including Press TV and Sky News, he has unapologetically criticized the Zionist lobby’s influence on US foreign policy, US military aggression against Iran, and the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
"When the US government starts a major war or national security agenda, they want to control the narrative," Azizi observed. "They pressure independent analysts to support their policies. If you don't, they attack you and put labels on you."
Family trauma and diplomatic intervention
The psychological toll on Azizi’s family was immense. He revealed that an FBI special agent threatened his wife on two occasions, attempting to use her and their young children as leverage to coerce Azizi into cooperating with US authorities.
While the local Iranian-American community and his children’s school rallied to support his family, the situation remained dire.
Azizi credited the Iranian Interests Section at the Pakistani Embassy in Washington, D.C., particularly its head, Abolfazl Mehrabadi, for intervening.
Despite the immense challenges, Mehrabadi and his team traveled to detention centers across the US, advocating for thousands of detained Iranian nationals and ultimately facilitating Azizi’s swift and safe return to Iran.
A call for justice
Now back in his home country, Azizi remains steadfast in his analytical approach.
He rejected the notion that he is an ideologue, stating that his role is to objectively evaluate policies, criticizing economic hardships in Iran just as he condemns US imperialism and Israeli aggression.
Regarding his academic future, Azizi is in communication with his committee chair at Virginia Tech to defend his dissertation remotely, a procedure that has precedents post-pandemic.
However, due to US sanctions, he may need to register from a third country, such as Turkey or the UAE, to complete his degree.
Azizi’s case is not an isolated incident. It reflects a broader, alarming pattern of politically driven immigration enforcement and due process violations targeting foreign nationals, particularly Iranians, in the United States.
A growing coalition of civil rights advocates, academics, and community members has launched a petition demanding a fair review of Azizi’s case and full accountability for the arbitrary nature of his detention.
Supporters emphasize that when no clear legal violation is presented, the detention serves only as a political tool to intimidate and silence dissent.

Likud Party threatens Central Elections Committee petition over Fly&Vote initiative
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:38:42 UTC
03:38:42 KST

The Likud Party is threatening to petition the Central Elections Committee and take legal action against the organizations behind the Fly&Vote initiative, which aims to help Israelis abroad travel to Israel to vote in the elections.
In a warning letter sent Sunday through attorney Ilan Bombach, Likud said the initiative's activities raise concerns about potential violations of election laws, particularly rules barring the provision of benefits to voters and attempts to influence how they vote.
The letter was sent, among others, to the America Israel Democracy (AID) Coalition, the "Israeli Camp," and parties involved in operating the AID Coalition. Likud is demanding that the organizations provide a series of documents and data related to the initiative's activities within five days and immediately halt any activity that the party says could influence the electoral process.
According to the letter, the initiative operates on a broad scale, with details of its activities made public through media interviews and various events. Likud's attorneys cited provisions of the Knesset Elections Law on "election bribery," arguing that providing services or benefits to citizens to influence their vote could constitute an offense.
One of Likud's main claims concerns information it says the organizations running the initiative hold. The letter alleges that a database contains identifying information about voters in the Knesset elections, as well as information about their voting intentions.
The letter also claims the initiative is working to transport voters on Election Day outside the framework established by law and is contacting voters to discourage them from voting for Likud's candidate list.
Likud further claims that the initiative's activities include publishing advertisements and election propaganda intended to influence voters. The party argues that the activities should also be examined under laws governing election propaganda and the financing of political activity, saying such activity cannot be carried out without considering the relevant legal requirements.
Likud seeks data, documents on Fly&Vote initiative
As part of its demands, Likud is seeking the data and documents on which the initiative's activities are based within five days, saying the material is needed to determine whether further legal action is warranted.
At the same time, the organizations have been instructed to immediately cease the activities, including any activities carried out jointly, remove related publications, and halt any other activity connected to the initiative.
Likud is also demanding that, by August 24, the organizations approach the chairman of the Central Elections Committee for the Knesset, request the necessary orders, and make any payment required by law for publications and activities the party claims are prohibited.
Letter sent by Likud in May demanded end to activities
The letter also refers to previous correspondence between the parties. In May, Likud sent a similar request demanding that the activities be stopped. The organizations responded, but Likud now claims that the explanations failed to address the allegations it raised.
If Likud's demands are not met, the party says it intends to petition the chairman of the Central Elections Committee and ask him to order the activities to be stopped. Likud is also reserving the right to pursue additional legal proceedings.

U.S. Sends NATO Allies Questionnaire on Loyalty Amid European Troop Cuts
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:36:58 UTC
03:36:58 KST

The administration of U.S. President Donald Trump has sent NATO allies a special questionnaire to assess their alignment with U.S. foreign policy.
Bloomberg reported this, citing a document obtained by the publication.
The document calls for an assessment of the political positions of member states in anticipation of possible cuts to the U.S. military presence in Europe.
The United States is asking its partners whether they have publicly supported U.S. foreign policy initiatives, including actions in the Middle East and the Western Hemisphere. The document also specifically asks about national restrictions on the use of military bases by U.S. forces.
A significant portion of the questionnaire focuses on defense procurement and allies’ defense spending. The United States wants to know whether countries purchase weapons from U.S. contractors and whether they have opposed “‘Made in Europe’ regulations” that restrict contracts with U.S. companies.
The document effectively ties U.S. security guarantees to the ideological and economic loyalty of its allies.
NATO allies reacted negatively to the demands, viewing them as an attempt to exert pressure and use security guarantees as leverage in exchange for political subordination.
The assessment concerns disagreements between the United States and Europe over strikes on Iran carried out without authorization, the detention of Venezuelan dictator Nicolás Maduro and the EU’s protectionist policy in the defense industry. In particular, following U.S. actions in Iran, some countries, including Spain, banned the use of their bases for the attacks.
The document directly asks countries that have imposed similar restrictions on the use of bases or weapons purchases whether they are willing to reduce or fully lift such bans. The assessment is expected to result in further cuts to the U.S. military presence in Europe.
The United States has already announced plans to withdraw 5,000 troops from Germany and redeploy other forces without replacing them. At the same time, Donald Trump promised to send an additional contingent to Poland after Karol Nawrocki was elected president.
The cuts could affect not only personnel but also U.S. military equipment intended to protect allies in the event of an attack. Strategic bombers, which European countries do not have, as well as strike drones and warships, could also be affected by the cuts.
A NATO representative confirmed that the United States is working with allies to review its military presence but declined to comment on the document itself. The Pentagon also did not provide official comment on the questionnaire that was sent.

The aged care algorithm deciding support for older Australians
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:36:57 UTC
03:36:57 KST

Inside the aged care algorithm deciding support for older Australians
The last time 96-year-old Audrey Staniland was assessed for in-home aged care funding was with a human clinician more than a decade ago.
When her daughter applied for a reassessment late last year, hoping Audrey would receive a higher level of care, she knew a clinician would assess her, but would not make the final decision.
Instead, a "classification algorithm" would be deciding the outcome, with the clinician unable to change it.
The algorithm was introduced in November and has been mired in controversy ever since.
The government has resisted calls from the opposition and crossbenchers to hand over documents about its design.
Australia's pre-eminent expert on health care algorithms, Kathy Eagar, has unpacked the algorithm's opaque workings and is adamant about what should happen next.
"It can only be fixed by ditching the whole algorithm and starting again, if you think that it's better to have an algorithm [rather] than an expert clinical assessor determine what a person needs," she said.
Using Professor Eagar's expert analysis, evidence revealed by bureaucrats at Senate estimates, and documents obtained under Freedom of Information, a Four Corners investigation can reveal the fullest picture yet of the secretive algorithm affecting the lives of tens of thousands of older Australians and their families.
'It was a tick and flick'
It was January 20 when a clinical assessor came to Audrey's Perth home of 43 years.
She brought a laptop containing an electronic questionnaire known as the Integrated Assessment Tool.
"I was very worried about a computer making a decision on a human being [rather than] the person in the room [who] could see Mum's condition," Audrey's daughter, Jan Helgeland, said.
Jan had arranged for Audrey to have a reassessment because her provider had increased its hourly rate for services such as personal care and social support from $90 to $115, meaning Audrey had to cut back on care.
Jan was hoping her mother would be approved for a new, higher level of funding to restore the hours of care she had lost.
"I think what she's missing out on most of all is having someone in the house here with her," Jan said.
Jan said the assessor sat at the kitchen counter and asked Audrey questions.
She put them into the Integrated Assessment Tool, a questionnaire containing more than 500 questions, including more than 100 text boxes for notes.
She asked Audrey about her daily life, watched how she moved around the house with her walker, and took notes about her health conditions such as her blindness due to macular degeneration and her emphysema.
"She would ask the question and then tap away on the laptop," Jan said.
"It was a tick and flick."
Two days later, Audrey received her outcome. Despite her conditions, age and the fact she lives alone, the classification algorithm decided she should remain on the same level of funding she'd received nearly 12 years earlier.
Audrey and Jan were shocked.
"I was gobsmacked," Jan said.
"They say they want to keep you in your home, but why are they making it so damned hard?" Audrey added.
"You'd think they'd be making it a bit easier for you, but they're not."
Unpacking the black box
With Audrey's permission, we were able to obtain her assessment with the answers and notes put in by the assessor.
We took them to Professor Eagar to analyse. Professor Eagar is an honorary professor of health services research at the University of New South Wales and has unpacked the black box for Four Corners.
"How can this frail old lady with all these problems get less hours … the answer is the way the algorithm works," Professor Eagar said.
Professor Eagar said, like any algorithm, this one worked like a tree with branches.
On the first branch, a person receives a "functional score" based on their ability to perform daily activities such as showering, preparing meals, and getting around.
On the second branch, they are scored on whether their need to complete those tasks is being met fully, partially or not at all.
The third branch is where the person is scored on so-called "compounding factors" such as frailty, cognitive problems and mental health.
The person's scores are then put through the classification algorithm, whose formula is set out in complex legislation in the Aged Care Rules 2024.
That formula determines, if eligible, the amount of funding the person receives, from level one to eight.
Professor Eagar said there were numerous problems, but a key flaw was that crucial questions — about cognition, frailty, and other health conditions — were considered too late in the decision tree to have an impact.
"It's the first really fundamental error, and it shapes everything else," Professor Eagar said.
"Even though those things come in later, it's too late. They come in at a point where their impact in the model is absolutely immaterial."
Professor Eagar said the other big problem was that, although the questionnaire included more than 500 questions, the vast majority of responses were not considered by the algorithm.
This includes more than 100 free text boxes in which assessors record important details about someone's life, which are not read by the algorithm.
"This huge assessment tool, we ask all these questions, most of which are completely ignored," Professor Eagar said.
Aged Care Minister Sam Rae told Four Corners that the algorithm drew on the data it needed.
"The classification and prioritisation mechanisms draw the data that they need in order to get the best outcome for all the people," he said.
Professor Eagar said the algorithm was also statistically flawed because at one branch in the decision tree, a single point in a person's score could mean they gained or lost almost $40,000 a year in funding.
Appealing against the algorithm
After receiving the results, Audrey's daughter, Jan, appealed against the algorithm's decision to deny Audrey increased funding.
To do this, she was required to write and post a letter to the department at a South Australian post office box. However, people can now email their requests for review.
Audrey never received a response, with the department telling her daughter that if she did not hear from it within 90 days, her appeal had been unsuccessful.
Professor Eagar compared the appeals process to the Robodebt scheme, in which people on income support were incorrectly issued with automatically generated debt notices and were forced to disprove the debts.
"Because in Robodebt and here, the onus is on the consumer, the frail older person, they then have to challenge the algorithm," she said.
"Nobody has to justify why the algorithm gave them that."
In the first five months of the algorithm's use, more than 1,000 people have asked for reviews. That is a six-fold increase on requests for review in 2024-25. Of about 900 reviewed, 207 were successful.
Mr Rae said the number of review requests represented less than half a per cent of the more than 250,000 Australians who were assessed in the first half of 2026.
"No single system will get everything right, of course, so we need a robust review process, but in terms of a proportion of the overall workload, half a per cent is, to my mind, a relatively tolerable number," he said.
Jan applied for another assessment for her mother, but once again the algorithm said no to more funding.
"I don't think this government actually realises the pressure and the stress that it's putting on the elderly and the people around them," Jan said.
Audrey said she would "do anything to stay" in her home.
"I don't want to go into a [nursing] home," she said.
"Not being able to see, I wouldn't know … where I was or … how to get around or anything. I know everything here where I can go from room to room."
'Beyond what you should expect a generic public servant to ever do'
The algorithm was introduced by the government to ensure consistent funding because it said some assessors were over-funding elderly people, leading to a surplus of $4 billion in unspent funds.
Private consultants designed the original algorithm, but the version used today was finalised and validated by public servants in the Department of Health and Ageing.
According to Professor Eagar, that is why there are so many problems.
"They should never have been asked to do a job that is so technically sophisticated," she said.
"It's beyond what you should expect a generic public servant to ever do."
A 2023 report obtained under FOI warned that developing the classification algorithm would be "a relatively complex modelling exercise for the department".
The report said any model developed would need to be "performance tested" to consider "whether the funding results are fair and justifiable" and to ensure results "can be vetted by subject matter … experts."
However, at Senate estimates, under questioning by the Coalition, Greens and independent senator David Pocock, the department admitted there had been no live trial of the final algorithm and it was unable to name any expert clinicians who validated it.
The department maintains that the algorithm is functioning correctly, and that it has been tested on more than 200,000 assessments from 2024-25 to ensure it achieves reliable outcomes and consistent care.
The opposition and crossbenchers passed a bill in the Senate last month giving assessors the ability to override the algorithm, but last week it was rejected by the government in the lower house.
Mr Rae said the government would "legislate a new assessment escalation pathway", allowing assessment agencies to ask for reviews of decisions when necessary.
The department has confirmed the May budget had committed funding to review and refine the algorithm.
"I want to see the very best outcomes for older Australians," Mr Rae said.
"Investing in constant improvement is a critical way to make sure that the $50 billion of precious taxpayer money that we will be expending each financial year over the coming financial years is invested to the very best that it can be."
Watch Four Corners' full investigation, The Waiting Game, from 8:30pm Monday on ABC TV and ABC iview.

Calls for UK inquiry into ‘hounding’ of ex-Cambridge academic
- Over 31,000 people, including MPs, have petitioned UK PM Andy Burnham to hold a public inquiry into alleged media harassment of late Cambridge academic Jason Arday.
- Arday faced plagiarism allegations and racial abuse linked to his work and background, which many believe contributed to his tragic death.
- Friends and supporters warned media about suicide risks; a vigil and fundraising campaign have been organised to honour Arday's memory and support his family.
AI generated
LONDON – More than 31,000 people, including several MPs, have signed a petition urging British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to hold a public inquiry into alleged media harassment of the late academic Jason Arday, the organisers said on Aug 16.
The Good Law Project activist group launched the petition after Arday, who was appointed three years ago as the youngest-ever black professor at Cambridge University, was found dead on Aug 14.
The project had been supporting the 41-year-old since he resigned earlier in August from the university and as a fellow of Jesus College after both institutions launched investigations into allegations of plagiarism and fabricating or exaggerating his life story.
“There cannot be any doubt that Dr Arday’s tragic death was the direct, foreseeable and foreseen result of press harassment,” the Good Law Project wrote on its website.
“A significant element in that harassment was the colour of his skin,” it said, adding that “there cannot be any doubt that racism lay at the heart of this story”.
The allegations against Arday received widespread media coverage in the British press after another academic – self-defined “race realist” Nathan Cofnas, who was sacked from his Cambridge role in 2024 – said in July that he found numerous instances of plagiarism in the professor’s work.
British media and right-wing commentators seized on the row, claiming Arday, who disputed the allegations, had unfairly benefited from diversity, equality and inclusion policies.
Warnings of ‘suicide risk’
In a letter published when he resigned on Aug 5, Arday said the move was “the only way” to end a “difficult period”, but should not be “mistaken for an acceptance of the narratives that have surrounded me”.
Following the shock news of his death on Aug 14, which the police are not treating as suspicious, his family and friends have denounced “a campaign of sustained abuse” since his 2023 appointment.
Other friends have said he was vulnerable, given that Arday has written extensively about being diagnosed with autism as a child and not speaking until he was 11.
Simon Woolley, Arday’s former mentor and a leading member of staff at Cambridge University, told the BBC on Aug 16 that he and a group of friends had seen him on Aug 10.
Arday “said he felt hounded to death, his words, that he couldn’t see a way out”, Woolley said.
“On that day, we saw a man half his body weight and desperate beyond belief.”
The Good Law Project said “many of the signatories” to its campaign had “warned multiple media outlets privately that their relentless pursuit of Dr Arday risked his suicide”.
A vigil for the late academic is set to be held in London’s Trafalgar Square on the evening of Aug 17.
A fund-raising campaign to support his family has already raised almost £89,000 (S$154,000). AFP

‘It’s been very tough’: hope of progress in gruelling battle against south Wales wildfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-16
18:27:39 UTC
03:27:39 KST

More than three weeks after it began burning and two days after the military deployed to the area, there is hope that the huge wildfire on the hillside above the Ebbw valley village of Blaenavon may finally be coming under control.
Emergency workers and soldiers described a gruelling battle against the deep-seated peat fire that has spread over 4,000 hectares (9,800 acres), putting lives, farmland and property at risk.
At least 13 other fires have blazed across the valleys this weekend, prompting South Wales fire and rescue service to ask for military support – the first UK military deployment to deal with wildfires since 2018.
Nationally, approximately 36 fires are still burning, 11 of which have been declared major incidents. Extreme heat and a lack of rain, supercharged by the climate crisis, have made this summer the busiest on record for wildfires in the UK, placing significant pressure on crews and resources.
Jamie Windsor, a group commander at Ebbw Vale station, said underground layers of peat beneath the orange and purple heather on the Blaenavon hillside had made the fire harder to put out.
“It burns very deep, the peat, and because it’s been so hot, it’s not cooling down at night. You think you’ve got a handle on it but it’s burning underground and it just pops up again somewhere else,” he said. “We’re got a lot of wildfire experience here in south Wales but I’ve never seen anything like it in 30 years.”
During the Guardian’s visit to the scene on Sunday, soldiers from the Queen’s Own Gurkha Logistic Regiment tirelessly dug firebreaks and turned over smoking soil to minimise the spread of fire. Small flames licked around the base of blackened trees a few metres away as they worked, while in another part of the woods several trees lit up quickly with no warning.
On the ridge of the hill, a civilian-contracted helicopter picked up water from a huge plastic pool fed by a local dam and circled again and again to dowse reigniting pockets of the smouldering hillside.
Smoke from the area has been visible as far away as Cardiff and Gloucestershire. Firefighters from services around the UK have come to help improvise how to get water to hard-to-reach places, using an old steel mill on the edge of town as a temporary headquarters. New thermal camera drones and specialised response vehicles designed by the South Wales fire service came online this summer.
“Just in time,” said Darren Cleaves, the group manager for the service, as he radioed a colleague at the perimeter of the fire to report what he could see on the drone screen. “The drone means we can be much more accurate with pinpointing where we need to go, and it keeps our teams safer.”
The combined efforts have worked, saving houses in Blaenavon a few hundred metres away. For weeks, residents on Llanover Close, a road on the village boundary, have watched a steady stream of fire engines, water tankers, tractors and other emergency vehicles and equipment go back and forth to the forestry track above their homes.
Cindy Rogers, 60, lives in the last house on the road where Blaenavon meets the hillside. A fire in 2004 that began on the top of the mountain almost reached her house, she said, pointing from her back garden to where the fire line is still visible.
“It’s a worry that this is going to get worse in the future with climate change, but I wouldn’t move unless I really had to,” she said. “All it takes is the wind to change direction and that’s it.”
By Sunday afternoon, the Blaenavon fire was showing signs it may be slowing, said Fin Monahan, the chief fire officer of South Wales fire and rescue.
“It’s been very tough, but I’m so proud of the professionalism of these teams and how hard they are working,” he said. “Morale is still high, everything is calm and controlled … It’s just the scale of what we’re dealing with is unprecedented. We normally get about 1,000 999 calls a week, and at the moment it’s 7,000.”
Arson had been a major contributor to this summer’s fires, Monahan said. “Not every investigation has been completed yet but we can already see it’s been a significant issue this year in south Wales. Fire safety education is another key area we focus on … Driving home last night, I saw smoke and I went and found a guy burning tires and other stuff in his garden, under a tree. I had to tell him to put it out.”
The cause of the Blaenavon fire is still unknown, but across the country arson arrests have been made in relation to this summer’s fires. On Saturday, four teenage boys from Porth in the Rhondda valley were detained on suspicion of arson and later released on bail.
In Stoke-on-Trent, a man and woman have been arrested in connection to a fire that destroyed four homes, and a man in King’s Norton and another in east London have been arrested on suspicion of arson to endanger life.
The UK has experienced multiple heatwaves this summer, as climate breakdown makes extreme heat, drought and wildfires more likely. The whole of Wales and almost three-quarters of England were declared officially in drought last month, and the Met Office said this week that the UK was on course for its hottest summer on record by average temperature.
The Blaenavon fire and many others across the country may only finally settle with cooler temperatures and rain, but the onset of autumn and more rainfall is not guaranteed to reverse the drought conditions, the Met Office said on Saturday.
In Blaenavon, flash flooding has plagued residents in recent years. A supercharged El Niño is now predicted to bring wet and stormy conditions to the UK this winter.
An 89-year-old resident of Llanover Close, who did not want to give his name, said he had lived on the street since it was built. “It’s the flooding that worries me. My basement flooded last winter,” he said. “Fire and flood … I never thought it would come to this.”
